question: Read the passage: Officers must complete a use-of-force report before the end of the shift in which force was used. The report goes to the shift supervisor, who reviews it within 72 hours and forwards it to the training unit. If the supervisor finds that the force may have violated policy, the report goes to internal affairs instead of the training unit. According to the passage, when does a report go to internal affairs?
optionA: When force may have broken policy
optionC: When the officer adds a supplement
optionD: When the training unit requests it
explanation: The passage sends a report to internal affairs only when the supervisor finds the force may have violated policy. The 72-hour review time and supplements have nothing to do with where the report goes.

question: Read the passage: Property and evidence must be packaged separately. Each item gets its own bag or container, sealed with evidence tape, and the sealing officer writes initials and the date across the tape. Firearms are unloaded before packaging. Wet items, such as bloody clothing, are air-dried before they are sealed, because sealing them wet can destroy biological evidence. Why does the passage say wet items are dried before sealing?
optionA: To make the tape stick properly
optionC: To reduce the weight of the bag
optionD: To keep the items from smelling
explanation: The passage gives one reason: sealing wet items can destroy biological evidence. The other options may sound sensible but are not stated.

question: Read the passage: When officers arrive at a disturbance call, one officer speaks with each party in a separate area, out of sight and hearing of the other. Separating the parties lets each person speak freely. Officers then compare the two accounts with what any witnesses saw and with the physical evidence before deciding what happened. Which reason for separating the parties does the passage give?
optionA: So the scene can be photographed
optionB: So each person can be searched
optionC: So each person can speak freely
optionD: So the officers can finish faster
explanation: The passage says separation lets each person speak freely. Photographs, searches and speed are not mentioned.

question: Read the passage: A vehicle pursuit may be started only when the officer has reason to believe the driver has committed a violent felony. The officer must end the pursuit if the risk to the public becomes greater than the need to catch the suspect, or when a supervisor orders it. Pursuits for traffic violations, stolen property or misdemeanors are not allowed under this policy. Under this policy, which situation allows a pursuit to begin?
optionA: A driver who ran a red light
optionB: A driver who stole a car
optionC: A driver with a suspended license
optionD: A driver who just shot someone
explanation: Only a violent felony allows a pursuit, and a shooting is one. The passage rules out traffic violations and stolen property.

question: Read the passage: There is no waiting period before a missing person report is taken. Officers take the report as soon as it is made, whether the person has been gone for one hour or one week. Reports involving children under 13, people with dementia, or anyone who may be in danger are treated as high-risk and are broadcast to all units at once. Which case does the passage treat as high-risk?
optionA: A man with dementia missing an hour
explanation: People with dementia are high-risk no matter how long they have been gone. Time missing alone does not make a case high-risk under the passage.

question: Read the passage: At 2:10 a.m. Officer Reyes found the rear door of a hardware store open. The lock was undamaged and nothing appeared to be missing. The owner said by phone that the last employee to leave had closed at 9 p.m. and was new to the job. The owner came to the store, checked the stock and the cash drawer, and locked the door. Which conclusion is best supported by the passage?
optionA: A burglar forced the door open
optionB: The door was likely left unlocked
optionC: Cash was taken from the drawer
explanation: An undamaged lock, nothing missing and a new employee closing up all point to a door left unlocked. Nothing supports forced entry or theft.

question: Read the passage: Officers must turn on their body-worn camera before arriving at any call for service and keep it recording until they leave the scene. An officer may stop recording while speaking with a victim of sexual assault who asks not to be recorded, but must state the reason aloud before turning the camera off. Failing to record is reported to the officer's supervisor. Before turning off the camera for a victim who asks, the officer must:
optionB: Have the victim sign a form
explanation: The passage requires the officer to state the reason aloud before turning the camera off. Supervisor approval and a signed form are not required.

question: Read the passage: Most residential burglaries in the city happen between 10 a.m. and 3 p.m. on weekdays, when homes are most likely to be empty. Burglars usually enter through an unlocked door or window rather than by force. Because of this, the crime prevention unit spends most of its effort urging residents to lock doors and windows, even when they leave for a short time. Why does the unit focus on getting residents to lock up?
optionC: Forced entry is the most common method
explanation: The passage links the lock-up message to the fact that burglars usually walk in through unlocked doors and windows. It says burglaries happen mostly in the daytime, not at night.

question: Read the passage: During a traffic stop at night, officers park the patrol car about one car length behind the stopped vehicle and slightly to the left, so the patrol car shields the officer from passing traffic. Spotlights are aimed at the stopped car's mirrors, which makes it hard for the driver to see the officer walk up. According to the passage, the patrol car is offset to the left to:
optionC: Block the car from driving off
optionD: Give the driver room to exit
explanation: The offset is there so the patrol car shields the officer from passing traffic. Lighting the mirrors is the job of the spotlights, not the offset.

question: Read the passage: Juveniles taken into custody are kept out of sight and sound of adult prisoners at all times. A juvenile may be held in a secure room for no more than six hours while officers find a parent or guardian. If no parent can be found in that time, the officer contacts the on-call juvenile probation officer for instructions. What does the officer do if no parent is found within six hours?
optionA: Moves the youth to the adult cells
optionC: Releases the youth to a neighbor
optionD: Holds the youth for another six hours
explanation: The passage says to contact the on-call juvenile probation officer. Holding longer than six hours or mixing with adults breaks the stated rules.

question: Read the passage: Officers should use plain language in reports. Words such as "proceeded" and "observed" can be replaced with "went" and "saw." Short sentences in the order events happened are easier for prosecutors and juries to follow. Abbreviations should be spelled out the first time they are used. Which change does the passage recommend?
optionA: Writing events in order of importance
explanation: The passage gives went for proceeded as an example of plain language. It asks for time order, short sentences and spelling out abbreviations the first time.

question: Read the passage: Latent prints are invisible prints left by oils and sweat on a surface. Smooth, non-porous surfaces such as glass and painted metal are usually dusted with powder. Porous surfaces such as paper and cardboard absorb the oils, so prints on them are developed with chemicals in the lab instead of powder at the scene. According to the passage, how should prints on a cardboard box be handled?
optionA: Dusted with powder at the scene
optionB: Lifted with tape at the scene
optionC: Dusted after the box dries out
explanation: Cardboard is porous, and the passage says porous items are developed with chemicals in the lab. Powder is for smooth surfaces like glass.

question: Read the passage: During the parade, officers on foot are assigned to fixed posts along the route and must not leave them except to handle an emergency at or near the post. Officers who need a break notify the sector sergeant, who sends a relief officer. Lost children are taken to the first-aid tent at the end of the route, where parents are told to check. According to the passage, where does a lost child go?
explanation: The passage says lost children go to the first-aid tent at the end of the route. The sector sergeant handles relief for breaks.

question: Read the passage: Before a vehicle is entered as stolen in the state system, the officer confirms with the owner that the car was not repossessed, towed or borrowed by a family member. Many vehicles reported stolen turn out to have been towed. Entering a vehicle that is not stolen can lead to an innocent driver being stopped at gunpoint. Why does the officer check for a tow or repossession first?
optionA: To find the vehicle more quickly
optionB: To avoid stops of innocent drivers
optionC: To charge the owner a towing fee
optionD: To save the owner an insurance claim
explanation: The passage warns that a wrong stolen entry can get an innocent driver stopped at gunpoint. Fees and insurance are not mentioned.

question: Read the passage: When a person appears to be in a mental health crisis, officers slow the encounter down when it is safe to do so. They give the person space, speak calmly, use the person's name and avoid giving several commands at once. A crisis team clinician can be asked to respond with officers during daytime hours. Which approach fits the passage?
optionA: Giving several fast commands at once
optionC: Calm speech, one request at a time
optionD: Waiting for a clinician at night
explanation: The passage asks for calm speech and warns against several commands at once. It says to give space, and clinicians are available in the daytime.

question: Read the passage: In one county, a search warrant must be served within ten days of being issued. After the search, the officer leaves a copy of the warrant and a receipt for any property taken at the place searched. The officer then returns the warrant to the court with an inventory of the property. What must the officer leave at the place searched?
optionA: The inventory sent to the court
optionB: A list of officers who searched
optionC: A business card and phone number
optionD: A warrant copy and a receipt
explanation: The passage says a copy of the warrant and a receipt are left at the place searched. The inventory goes back to the court.

question: Read the passage: Officers may not work more than 16 hours in any 24-hour period, counting regular shifts, overtime and off-duty jobs. After working 16 hours, an officer must have at least 8 hours off before returning to duty. Supervisors check hours before approving any overtime. An officer has worked a 12-hour shift. How many more hours may she work in that 24-hour period?
explanation: The limit is 16 hours in 24, and 16 minus 12 is 4. The 8 hours in the passage is the minimum rest period, not the hours left to work.

question: Read the passage: When showing a photo lineup, the officer who presents the photos should not know which photo is the suspect. The witness is told that the person may or may not be in the lineup and that the investigation will continue either way. The witness's confidence is written down in the witness's own words right after any identification. Why should the presenting officer not know which photo is the suspect?
optionA: So the lineup can be done faster
optionB: So no cues are given to the witness
optionC: So the officer can testify later
optionD: So the witness feels more confident
explanation: An officer who does not know the suspect cannot give hints, even by accident. That is the purpose of a blind lineup; speed and confidence are not the reason.

question: Read the passage: Radio traffic should be brief. Officers wait for a clear channel, identify themselves by unit number and give their location first, because if the transmission is cut off, the location is the most important detail. Emergency traffic takes priority over all other transmissions. According to the passage, why is the location given first?
optionA: It is the shortest part to say
optionC: It matters most if the call drops
optionD: It clears the channel for others
explanation: The passage says location goes first because it is the most important detail if the transmission is cut off. The unit number is what identifies the officer.

question: Read the passage: Bicycle patrol officers cover the downtown area from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. In bad weather, they switch to foot patrol rather than return to the station. Bicycle officers are especially useful in crowds and parks, where patrol cars cannot easily go, and they can often approach quietly. What do bicycle officers do in bad weather?
explanation: The passage says they switch to foot patrol rather than return to the station. Patrol cars are not mentioned as a bad-weather option.

question: Read the passage: At a collision scene, the first duty is to protect the scene and the people in it: park to block traffic, turn on emergency lights and check for injuries. Only after the injured are cared for and the scene is safe do officers take measurements and statements. Vehicles are moved only when they block traffic and only after photographs of their positions have been taken. Before vehicles are moved, the passage says officers must:
optionA: Photograph where they came to rest
optionB: Get written statements from both drivers
optionD: Wait for the tow trucks to arrive
explanation: The passage allows moving vehicles only after their positions are photographed. Statements and measurements come later and are not a condition for moving them.

question: Read the passage: Officers in a foot pursuit should broadcast their direction of travel and a description of the suspect. Officers should not split up from a partner, follow a suspect into a building alone, or keep going once they have lost sight of the suspect. In those cases they set up a perimeter and wait for help. A suspect runs into a warehouse and a lone officer loses sight of him. The passage says the officer should:
optionB: Set up a perimeter and wait
explanation: Losing sight of the suspect and facing a building alone are both cases where the passage says to set up a perimeter and wait for help.

question: Read the passage: Patrol officers carry naloxone nasal spray. If a person is unresponsive and an opioid overdose is suspected, the officer calls for medical help, gives one dose and starts rescue breathing or CPR as trained. If there is no response after two to three minutes, a second dose may be given. The person must be watched closely, since naloxone can wear off before the opioid does. Why does the passage say the person must be watched after naloxone?
optionA: It can cause a second overdose
optionB: It must be given every minute
optionC: It may wear off before the opioid
optionD: It works only after CPR starts
explanation: The passage says naloxone can wear off before the opioid does, so breathing can stop again. The second dose is given after two to three minutes, not every minute.

question: Read the passage: Reports written soon after an incident are more accurate than reports written days later. Memory fades quickly, and details such as times, distances and exact words spoken are the first to be lost. For this reason, officers take brief notes at the scene and write the full report before the end of the shift. What is the main idea of the passage?
optionA: Notes can replace a full report
optionB: Exact quotes belong only in notes
optionD: Write reports while memory is fresh
explanation: Every sentence supports writing the report soon, before memory fades. Notes are a help, not a replacement for the report.

question: Read the passage: A police dog may be used to track a suspect who has fled the scene of a felony. Before sending the dog into a building, the handler gives a loud warning, waits a reasonable time for the suspect to surrender and repeats the warning. Other officers stay behind the handler during a track so they do not lay down their own scent. Why do other officers stay behind the handler?
optionA: To avoid adding their own scent
optionB: To protect the dog from the suspect
optionD: To keep the dog from turning back
explanation: The passage says officers stay behind so they do not lay down their own scent, which could confuse the dog.

question: Read the passage: When a victim or witness speaks limited English, officers use a qualified interpreter, in person or by phone. Family members, and especially children, should not interpret except in an emergency, because they may change or soften what is said and may themselves be affected by the case. Why does the passage advise against using children as interpreters?
optionA: They cannot be paid for it
optionB: They may change what is said
optionC: Phone lines do not allow it
optionD: They must be in school then
explanation: The passage says family members, especially children, may change or soften what is said. Pay and school hours are not mentioned.

question: Read the passage: Every person who handles an item of evidence signs the chain-of-custody form with the date, the time and the reason for handling it. A gap in the chain does not automatically keep evidence out of court, but it gives the defense a reason to question whether the item was changed. According to the passage, a gap in the chain of custody:
optionA: Always keeps the item out of court
optionB: Means the item must be retested
optionC: Lets the defense question the item
optionD: Must be fixed by the prosecutor
explanation: The passage says a gap does not automatically exclude the evidence, but it lets the defense question whether the item was changed.

question: Read the passage: In the beat officer program, each officer is assigned to the same neighborhood for at least two years. Officers attend community meetings, learn the names of business owners and work with residents to solve repeat problems such as noise or abandoned cars. The goal is to prevent crime by fixing the conditions that lead to it, not only to respond after it happens. What is the goal of the program described?
optionD: Preventing crime by fixing its causes
explanation: The last sentence states the goal: prevent crime by fixing the conditions that lead to it. Officers stay in one area, so rotation is wrong.

question: Read the passage: If an officer arrives at a crash involving a truck with hazardous-materials placards, the officer stays upwind and uphill, at a distance, and reads the placard number with binoculars if possible. The officer must not walk into a vapor cloud or spill to rescue someone without protective equipment, but should direct people who can walk to move away. Where should the officer stay at the scene?
optionA: Upwind and uphill, at a distance
optionC: Beside the truck to block traffic
explanation: The passage says upwind, uphill and at a distance, reading the placard with binoculars. Downwind and downhill are where vapors and liquids travel.

question: Read the passage: Residents 18 and older may apply to ride with an officer for one shift. Applicants sign a waiver and pass a background check. Riders must stay in the car during high-risk calls and follow the officer's directions at all times. A person may ride no more than twice in a calendar year. A rider went out in March and in June. Can she ride again in October of the same year?
optionA: Yes, if she passes another check
optionB: No, the yearly limit is reached
optionC: Yes, if a new waiver is signed
optionD: No, riders may go only once
explanation: The limit is two rides per calendar year, and she has used both. The limit is two, not one.

question: Read the passage: Open-ended questions, such as asking a witness to describe what happened, let witnesses tell events in their own words and usually produce more information. Leading questions, which suggest an answer, can change what a witness remembers. Closed questions, which call for a short answer, are best saved for checking details at the end. Which question is best for opening a witness interview?
optionA: Was the car a red sedan?
optionB: Did he have a gun in his hand?
optionD: The man ran north, didn't he?
explanation: An open request lets the witness tell the story in their own words. The others are closed or leading questions that the passage saves for later or warns against.

question: Read the passage: Store security staff may detain a shoplifting suspect and call police. When officers arrive, they get a written statement from the employee who saw the theft, collect any video, and photograph the property before it is returned to the store. The merchandise does not need to be kept as evidence once it is photographed, unless it is damaged. When must the merchandise be kept as evidence?
optionA: When there is no video of it
optionC: When security staff ask for it
explanation: The passage keeps merchandise as evidence only when it is damaged. Otherwise a photograph is enough.

question: Read the passage: Officer Lin noted that the suspect's car hood was warm at 11:40 p.m., although the suspect said he had been home since 8 p.m. The night temperature was 40 degrees, and the car was parked outdoors in the driveway. What can best be inferred?
optionB: The suspect was home at 8 p.m.
optionC: The hood warms in cold weather
optionD: The car was parked in a garage
explanation: A hood that is still warm on a 40-degree night points to recent driving, which conflicts with the suspect's story. The car was outdoors, not in a garage.

question: Read the passage: For this policy, a critical incident is any event in which a person is seriously injured or killed as a result of police action, or in which an officer fires a weapon at a person, whether or not anyone is hit. After a critical incident, the officers involved are separated and give a full statement only after a rest period. Which event is a critical incident under this definition?
optionA: An officer's car is hit while parked
optionB: An officer fires at a person and misses
optionC: A suspect is bruised while handcuffed
optionD: An officer fires at a dangerous dog
explanation: Firing at a person counts whether or not anyone is hit. A bruise is not a serious injury, and the definition covers shots at people, not animals.

question: Read the passage: Patrol shifts run in three watches: day watch from 6 a.m. to 4 p.m., swing watch from 2 p.m. to midnight, and night watch from 10 p.m. to 8 a.m. The overlaps allow briefings and keep extra officers on the street during the busiest hours. At 3 p.m., which watches are on duty?
explanation: Day watch runs until 4 p.m. and swing watch starts at 2 p.m., so both are on at 3 p.m. Night watch does not start until 10 p.m.

question: Read the passage: Reports should record what the officer saw, heard and did, not the officer's opinions. Instead of writing that a driver was drunk, the officer should describe the signs: the odor of alcohol, slurred speech, unsteady balance, and red, watery eyes. The facts allow the reader to reach the conclusion. Which sentence follows the passage's advice?
optionB: He seemed like a heavy drinker.
optionC: He was clearly far too drunk to drive.
optionD: He swayed and his speech was slurred.
explanation: Swaying and slurred speech are observed signs. The other sentences state conclusions or opinions, which the passage says to avoid.

question: Read the passage: Animal control handles stray, injured and dead animals during business hours. After hours, patrol officers respond only to animals that are an immediate danger to people, such as a dog attacking someone, or to an animal hit by a car that is blocking a roadway. Other animal calls are logged for animal control the next morning. At 11 p.m. a caller reports a stray cat in her yard. What happens?
optionA: It is logged for the morning
optionD: The caller is told to trap it
explanation: A stray cat in a yard is not an immediate danger or a road hazard, so the call is logged for animal control the next morning.

question: Read the passage: Every year many officers die in traffic crashes. Wearing a seat belt, slowing down when responding to calls and staying alert at roadside stops are simple steps that save lives. The department's goal this year is full seat belt use on every shift. What is the main purpose of the passage?
optionA: To report this year's crash data
explanation: The passage lists safe habits and sets a seat belt goal, so its purpose is to persuade officers to drive safely. It gives no crash figures or laws.

question: Read the passage: Graffiti should be photographed and reported before it is removed. Repeated tags by the same writer can link many incidents to one suspect, which raises the total damage and can change how the case is charged. Property owners are asked to remove graffiti within 48 hours, since quick removal discourages new tagging. Why should graffiti be photographed before removal?
optionA: To prove the owner removed it
optionB: To show it was removed in 48 hours
optionC: To link tags to one suspect
optionD: To bill the owner for cleanup
explanation: Photos let investigators connect repeated tags to one writer, which matters for the charge. The 48-hour removal is about discouraging new tags.

question: Read the passage: During a building search, officers move slowly, clear one room at a time and mark rooms that have been cleared. They check places a person could hide, such as closets, crawl spaces and under beds, and never pass an uncleared doorway with their back to it. According to the passage, officers searching a building should:
optionC: Skip spaces too small to stand in
optionD: Clear one room at a time
explanation: The passage says to move slowly and clear one room at a time, including small hiding places such as crawl spaces.

question: In the sentence "The two suspects were held in ___ rooms," which spelling fills the blank?
explanation: Separate has an a in the middle: sep-a-rate. Seperate is one of the most common misspellings in reports.

question: In the sentence "The witness was reluctant to testify," the word reluctant most nearly means:
explanation: Reluctant means unwilling or hesitant. A reluctant witness does not want to testify.

question: Which sentence is written correctly?
optionA: The officers and me wrote the report.
optionB: Me and the officers wrote the report.
optionC: The officers and I wrote the report.
optionD: Myself and the officers wrote it.
explanation: I is the subject form. Drop the other people to test it: you would say I wrote the report, not me wrote the report.

question: In the sentence "The dispatcher did not ___ the call," which spelling fills the blank?
explanation: Receive follows the rule i before e except after c: re-c-ei-ve.

question: In the sentence "The suspect gave an evasive answer," the word evasive most nearly means:
explanation: An evasive answer avoids the question. Honest and detailed are close to the opposite.

question: Which verb correctly completes the sentence "Each of the witnesses ___ a statement"?
explanation: Each is singular, so it takes the singular verb has. The plural word witnesses sits in a phrase and does not change the subject.

question: In the sentence "The ___ approved the overtime request," which spelling fills the blank?
explanation: The rank is spelled lieu-ten-ant, with ie at the start and ant at the end.

question: In the sentence "The officer's account was corroborated by the video," the word corroborated most nearly means:
explanation: To corroborate is to support or confirm. Contradicted is the opposite.

question: Which word correctly completes the sentence "The patrol car had ___ lights on"?
explanation: Its with no apostrophe is the possessive. It's always means it is or it has, and its' is never correct.

question: In the sentence "It is unlawful to ___ a witness," which spelling fills the blank?
explanation: Harass has one r and a double s.

question: In the sentence "The man was apprehended two blocks away," the word apprehended most nearly means:
explanation: To apprehend a suspect is to arrest or seize him. Being spotted or questioned is less than being apprehended.

question: Which word correctly completes the sentence "___ going to the station after court"?
explanation: They're is the contraction of they are. There points to a place and their shows ownership.

question: In the sentence "The holding area can ___ ten prisoners," which spelling fills the blank?
explanation: Accommodate has a double c and a double m.

question: In the sentence "The victim's injuries were superficial," the word superficial most nearly means:
explanation: Superficial means on the surface and not serious. Internal and hidden injuries are the opposite.

question: Which word correctly completes the sentence "The suspect ___ the gun under the seat"?
explanation: The simple past of hide is hid. Hidden needs a helper verb, as in had hidden.

question: In the sentence "The collision ___ at the intersection," which spelling fills the blank?
explanation: Occurred has a double c and a double r. The r doubles because the stress falls on the last syllable of occur.

question: In the sentence "The sergeant gave an explicit order," the word explicit most nearly means:
explanation: Explicit means stated clearly and fully. Implied and hinted are the opposite.

question: Which word correctly completes the sentence "The injured man was ___ on the sidewalk"?
explanation: Lie means to recline and does not take an object, so a person is lying down. Lay needs an object, as in laying a bag on a table.

question: In the sentence "The team set up ___ on the house," which spelling fills the blank?
explanation: Surveillance has a double l and ends in ance.

question: In the sentence "The crowd became hostile," the word hostile most nearly means:
explanation: Hostile means unfriendly or aggressive. A frightened or confused crowd is not necessarily hostile.

question: Which of these is a complete sentence?
optionA: The car stopped at the light.
optionB: Because the car stopped at the light.
optionD: The car that stopped at the light.
explanation: It has a subject and a verb and stands alone. The others are fragments: one starts with because, one has no subject, and one has no main verb.

question: In the sentence "Use only the force that is ___," which spelling fills the blank?
explanation: Necessary has one c and a double s: ne-ces-sary.

question: In the sentence "The policy prohibits officers from accepting gifts," the word prohibits most nearly means:
explanation: To prohibit is to forbid. Discourages is weaker: it does not ban the act.

question: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
optionA: The door was open, the room was empty.
optionB: The door was open the room was empty.
optionC: The door, was open; the room was empty.
optionD: The door was open; the room was empty.
explanation: A semicolon can join two complete sentences. A comma alone makes a comma splice, and no punctuation makes a run-on.

question: In the sentence "The ___ ended when the car ran out of gas," which spelling fills the blank?
explanation: Pursuit starts with pur, like pursue, and ends in suit.

question: In the sentence "The detective found a discrepancy between the two statements," the word discrepancy most nearly means:
explanation: A discrepancy is a difference or conflict between things that should match.

question: Which pronoun correctly completes the sentence "The sergeant gave the award to Officer Kim and ___"?
explanation: After the preposition to, use the object form me. Drop Officer Kim to test it: gave the award to me.

question: In the sentence "The judge signed the ___ at noon," which spelling fills the blank?
explanation: Warrant has a double r and ends in ant.

question: In the sentence "Officers must remain impartial," the word impartial most nearly means:
explanation: Impartial means not favoring either side, so neutral is the match.

question: Which word correctly completes the sentence "The suspect was taller ___ his partner"?
explanation: Than is used for comparisons. Then refers to time.

question: In the sentence "The officer's ___ lasted an hour," which spelling fills the blank?
explanation: Testimony is spelled with an i after the t and ends in ony.

question: In the sentence "The neighbor's complaint was frivolous," the word frivolous most nearly means:
explanation: A frivolous complaint lacks a serious purpose or basis. Well founded is the opposite.

question: Which word correctly completes the sentence "She answered the questions ___"?
explanation: An adverb describes how she answered, and calmly is the adverb form.

question: In the sentence "The ___ was towed to the impound lot," which spelling fills the blank?
explanation: Vehicle ends in cle, like article.

question: In the sentence "The suspect was belligerent," the word belligerent most nearly means:
explanation: Belligerent means hostile and eager to fight or argue.

question: In the question "To ___ did you give the keys?", which word fills the blank?
explanation: Whom is the object form and follows the preposition to. Test it with him: you gave the keys to him.

question: In the sentence "A neighbor reported a ___ person," which spelling fills the blank?
explanation: Suspicious keeps the ci before ous: sus-pi-cious.

question: In the sentence "The officer took a cursory look at the trunk," the word cursory most nearly means:
explanation: A cursory look is hasty and not thorough. Careful and close are the opposite.

question: Which sentence uses capital letters correctly?
optionA: We drove North on Main street.
optionB: We drove north on main Street.
optionC: We drove north on Main Street.
optionD: we drove North on Main Street.
explanation: Street names are capitalized, compass directions are not when they give a direction, and every sentence starts with a capital.

question: In the sentence "The driver was ___ when medics arrived," which spelling fills the blank?
explanation: Conscious means awake and aware and has sc in the middle. Conscience is a different word meaning a sense of right and wrong.

question: Which sentence is clearest for a police report?
optionA: I saw Smith hit Jones with a bat.
optionB: He hit him with a bat, I saw it.
optionC: Jones was hit by him with the bat.
optionD: With a bat, he was hit by Smith.
explanation: It names who did what to whom. The others use he and him without saying who they mean.

question: A report says: "Officer Ruiz told Officer Lee that his car had a flat tire." Why is this sentence unclear?
optionB: It is not clear whose car it is
optionC: It is missing a time of day
optionD: It gives too many officers' names
explanation: His could mean Ruiz or Lee. A clear version names the owner, such as Lee's car.

question: An officer's notes read: (1) Arrested Lopez at 2215. (2) Dispatched to a fight at 2150. (3) Arrived at 2158. (4) Interviewed two witnesses at 2205. In time order, which event comes second?
explanation: By time: dispatched 2150, arrived 2158, interviews 2205, arrest 2215. Arrival is second.

question: Which statement belongs in a report as a fact?
optionA: The burglar was clearly a pro.
optionB: The owner seemed to be lying.
optionC: The thief must have known them.
explanation: A cut screen is something the officer can see and photograph. The others are guesses or opinions.

question: Which version is in the active voice?
optionB: The car was searched by Ali.
optionD: A search of the car was done.
explanation: In the active voice the person acting is the subject. The others are passive, and two of them hide who did the search.

question: Notes: victim Ann Cole, purse taken, 3:15 p.m., Elm Park, suspect ran east. Which sentence reports the notes accurately?
optionA: At 3:15 p.m. in Elm Park, Ann Cole took a purse and ran east.
optionB: At 3:15 p.m. in Elm Park, Ann Cole's purse was taken; the thief ran east.
optionC: At 5:15 p.m. in Elm Park, Ann Cole's purse was taken; the thief ran east.
optionD: At 3:15 p.m. in Elm Park, Ann Cole's purse was taken; the thief ran west.
explanation: It matches every note. The others make the victim the thief, change the time or change the direction.

question: Which detail is least needed in a residential burglary report?
optionA: Time the owner last left the home
optionB: A list of every item taken
optionD: Where and how entry was made
explanation: Entry point, items taken and the time the home was empty all help the investigation. Last week's weather does not.

question: Which sentence is the most concise?
optionA: The suspect fled on foot by running.
optionB: The suspect, on foot, fled away running.
optionC: The suspect ran away on his feet quickly.
explanation: It says the same thing in the fewest words, without repeating itself.

question: A witness said, word for word: "He had a knife and he said give me the money." How should the report record the threat?
explanation: A threat is key evidence, so the exact words go in quotation marks without changes.

question: Which sentence is best for a report that a jury will read?
optionA: The perp bailed from the whip.
optionB: The man ran from the car.
optionC: Subject exited the veh. on foot.
optionD: Dude took off from the car.
explanation: Plain English with no slang, jargon or abbreviations is easiest for a jury to follow.

question: Which sentence makes clear that the driver, not the officer, was drunk?
optionB: Being drunk, I stopped the driver.
optionC: I stopped the driver, who was drunk.
explanation: The clause who was drunk sits next to the driver. In the others the word drunk describes I, the officer.

question: Notes: the officer arrived, then heard a shot, then called for backup, then entered the building. Which event happened third?
explanation: The order is arrived, heard a shot, called for backup, entered. Calling for backup is third.

question: Which suspect description is most useful in a report?
optionC: A tall man who seemed sort of young
explanation: It gives sex, age, height and clothing that other officers can look for. The others are vague or opinions.

question: A department requires reports in the first person. Which sentence follows that rule?
explanation: First person means the writer says I. This officer, the writer and R/O (reporting officer) are third-person styles.

question: A report must use 24-hour time. An arrest at 9:40 p.m. is written as:
explanation: Add 12 to p.m. hours: 9 plus 12 is 21, so 2140. 0940 is the morning time.

question: Which sentence is the most objective?
optionA: The driver was a typical drunk.
optionB: The driver was rude and nasty.
explanation: Slurred speech is an observation. The other sentences are judgments about the person.

question: What is the main purpose of an incident report?
optionA: To record facts for later use
explanation: Reports preserve facts for investigators, prosecutors and courts. Courts decide guilt, and witnesses still testify.

question: Which entry gives the most exact location?
optionC: Upstairs at the Oak Street place
explanation: A street number with the apartment lets anyone find the exact place. The others could mean several buildings.

question: Which sentence should be left out of a bicycle theft report?
optionA: The bike had been locked to the rack.
optionB: The cable lock was found cut through.
optionC: The officer's lunch break was late.
optionD: The owner saw it at 9 a.m.
explanation: The lunch break has nothing to do with the theft. The lock and the last time the bike was seen are useful facts.

question: Put these in time order: (1) I arrived at 1410. (2) Dispatch sent me to a crash at 1402. (3) The tow truck arrived at 1435. (4) I checked both drivers for injuries at 1412. Which order is correct?
explanation: By the times: 1402 dispatch, 1410 arrival, 1412 injury check, 1435 tow truck.

question: Which sentence states the time most clearly?
optionB: The alarm sounded late at night.
explanation: An exact time is clear and can be checked. Late at night and after midnight cover hours.

question: Which is an observation rather than a conclusion?
optionC: He was guilty of the theft.
explanation: Shaking hands can be seen. Hiding something, guilt and his feelings are conclusions the officer draws.

question: Which phrase is redundant?
explanation: History is always in the past, so past adds nothing. Each of the others adds meaning.

question: In a typical incident report narrative, which comes first?
explanation: A narrative usually opens with how the officer got involved, such as a dispatch or an on-view stop, and then follows events in order.

question: Which sentence has parallel structure?
optionC: He ran, was jumping and hid.
explanation: All three verbs are in the same form. The others mix verb forms.

question: A witness says: "I was walking my dog when I heard glass break. I looked over and saw a teen in a gray hoodie climb out of the pharmacy window and run toward the bus stop." Which summary is accurate?
optionA: She saw a teen in gray break the window.
optionB: She saw a teen in gray leave by the window.
optionC: She saw a teen in gray run into the pharmacy.
optionD: She saw a man in gray leave by the door.
explanation: She heard the glass break but saw the teen climb out of the window. She did not see the window being broken.

question: Which sentence avoids an unsupported assumption?
optionA: A shoplifter ran from the store.
optionB: The thief ran from the store.
optionC: A woman ran from the store.
optionD: A guilty woman fled the store.
explanation: Shoplifter, thief and guilty all assume a crime the officer has not yet shown. Describe the person and what she did.

question: Which sentence is clear about who was injured?
optionA: Lee and Park fought, and he was hurt.
optionB: When Park pushed Lee, he got hurt.
optionC: He was hurt when he pushed him.
optionD: Lee was hurt when Park pushed him.
explanation: It names Lee as the injured person. In the others he could mean either man.

question: Which way of correcting an error in handwritten field notes is acceptable?
optionB: Blacking it out completely with ink
explanation: A single line keeps the original readable and the initials show who changed it. Hiding or removing notes looks like tampering.

question: A report that answers who, what, when, where, why and how is best described as:
explanation: Answering all six questions makes a report complete. Concise and objective are other qualities, and reports should not try to persuade.

question: In which tense are police report narratives usually written?
explanation: Reports describe events that have already happened, so they are written in the past tense.

question: The events were: the officer parked, saw smoke, then radioed for the fire department. Which sentence keeps that order?
optionA: I saw smoke, parked and radioed for fire.
optionB: I radioed for fire, parked and saw smoke.
optionC: I parked, radioed for fire and saw smoke.
optionD: I parked, saw smoke and radioed for fire.
explanation: Only this sentence lists parking, seeing smoke and radioing in the order they happened.

question: An officer drives at 45 miles per hour for 40 minutes. How far does she travel?
explanation: 40 minutes is 2/3 of an hour, and 45 times 2/3 is 30 miles.

question: Officers wrote 120 citations in March and 150 in April. What was the percent increase?
explanation: The increase is 30. Divide by the starting number: 30 / 120 = 0.25, or 25%. Dividing by 150 gives the wrong 20%.

question: A car was clocked at 68 mph in a 45 mph zone. How many miles per hour over the limit was it?
explanation: 68 minus 45 is 23.

question: Five officers worked 8, 10, 9, 12 and 11 hours of overtime. What was the average?
explanation: The total is 50 hours, and 50 divided by 5 officers is 10.

question: A shift starts at 10:00 p.m. and lasts 10 hours. When does it end?
explanation: Two hours takes the shift to midnight, and eight more hours makes 8:00 a.m.

question: Evidence includes 3 bags of 28 pills each and 1 bag of 16 pills. How many pills are there in all?
explanation: 3 times 28 is 84, and 84 plus 16 is 100.

question: A skid mark measures 18 yards. How many feet is that?
explanation: There are 3 feet in a yard, so 18 times 3 is 54 feet.

question: A city of 80,000 people had 240 burglaries last year. What was the rate per 1,000 people?
explanation: 80,000 is 80 thousands, and 240 divided by 80 is 3 burglaries per 1,000 people.

question: A department has 150 officers, and 18% are on leave. How many officers are on leave?
explanation: 0.18 times 150 is 27. 123 is the number still working.

question: A patrol car uses 1 gallon of fuel every 15 miles. How much fuel does a 210-mile shift use?
explanation: 210 divided by 15 is 14 gallons.

question: Day calls and night calls were in a ratio of 3 to 2. There were 250 calls in all. How many were at night?
explanation: The ratio has 5 parts, so each part is 250 / 5 = 50. Night is 2 parts, or 100.

question: A suspect ran 0.3 miles in 2 minutes. What was his speed in miles per hour?
explanation: 0.3 miles in 2 minutes is 0.15 miles per minute, and 0.15 times 60 minutes is 9 mph.

question: An officer has 4 hours to write reports and finishes one report every 20 minutes. How many reports can she finish?
explanation: 4 hours is 240 minutes, and 240 divided by 20 is 12.

question: Arrests fell from 400 one year to 340 the next. What was the percent decrease?
explanation: The drop is 60, and 60 / 400 = 0.15, or 15%.

question: Three quarters of 48 recruits passed firearms qualification on the first try. How many did not?
explanation: Three quarters of 48 is 36 who passed, so 48 minus 36 is 12 who did not.

question: A patrol car's odometer read 24,385 at the start of a shift and 24,512 at the end. How many miles were driven?
A room is 12 feet by 15 feet. What is its area?
explanation: Area is length times width: 12 times 15 is 180 square feet. 54 is the perimeter in feet.

question: Officers tape off a square block that is 300 feet on each side. How much tape goes around the outside?
explanation: A square has 4 equal sides, so 4 times 300 is 1,200 feet. 90,000 is the area in square feet.

question: Response times were 5, 3, 8, 12 and 4 minutes. What is the median?
explanation: In order the times are 3, 4, 5, 8, 12, and the middle value is 5. 6.4 is the mean.

question: A car is moving at 88 feet per second. One mile per hour is about 1.47 feet per second. About how fast is the car in miles per hour?
explanation: Divide by 1.47: 88 / 1.47 is about 60 mph. Multiplying instead gives the wrong 129.

question: Twelve officers share 3 cases of water with 24 bottles in each case. How many bottles does each officer get?
explanation: 3 cases of 24 is 72 bottles, and 72 divided by 12 is 6.

question: An academy lasts 960 hours of training. At 40 hours a week, how many weeks does it take?
explanation: 960 divided by 40 is 24.

question: Two fifths of 85 calls were traffic-related. How many calls were traffic-related?
explanation: 85 divided by 5 is 17, and 2 times 17 is 34. 51 is the other three fifths.

question: An incident started at 1347 and ended at 1522. How long did it last?
explanation: From 1347 to 1447 is 1 hour, and 1447 to 1522 is 35 minutes.

question: A jail serves 18 prisoners 3 meals a day for 2 days. How many meals is that?
explanation: 18 times 3 is 54 meals a day, and 54 times 2 days is 108.

question: A suspect is 6 feet 2 inches tall. What is his height in inches?
explanation: 6 feet is 72 inches, and 72 plus 2 is 74.

question: A seized substance weighs 2.5 kilograms. One kilogram is 1,000 grams. How many grams is that?
explanation: 2.5 times 1,000 is 2,500 grams.

question: A plaza is 50 feet by 80 feet. If each person takes up about 4 square feet, about how many people can it hold?
explanation: The area is 50 times 80, or 4,000 square feet, and 4,000 divided by 4 is 1,000 people.

question: Of 260 emergency calls, 221 were answered in under 5 minutes. What percent is that?
explanation: 221 divided by 260 is 0.85, or 85%.

question: One officer can search a field alone in 6 hours, and another can search it alone in 3 hours. How long does it take them working together?
explanation: Together they search 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/2 of the field each hour, so the whole field takes 2 hours.

question: A breath test reads 0.12, and the limit used is 0.08. By what percent does the reading exceed the limit?
explanation: The reading is 0.04 over. 0.04 divided by the limit of 0.08 is 0.5, or 50%. Dividing by 0.12 gives the wrong 33%.

question: An officer starts with 40 rounds, fires 13 at the range, then fires 9 more. How many rounds remain?
explanation: 13 plus 9 is 22 rounds fired, and 40 minus 22 is 18.

question: On a burglary call you see a fellow officer take cash from the scene and put it in his pocket. What should you do?
optionB: Talk to him later in private
optionC: Ignore it unless it happens again
optionD: Write it in your notes only
explanation: Theft by an officer is serious misconduct and must be reported up the chain. Handling it privately or staying quiet makes you part of it.

question: A store owner offers you a free meal for keeping an eye on the place. What should you do?
optionA: Accept it once to be friendly
optionD: Accept but pay half the price
explanation: Gifts tied to extra police service create a duty to the giver. Decline politely; the store gets the same service as everyone else.

question: Driving to a minor theft report, you see a person collapse on the sidewalk. What should you do?
optionC: Help the person and call medics
explanation: A possible medical emergency outranks a minor property report. Stop, tell dispatch, get medics coming and give aid.

question: A man yells insults at you while you write a parking ticket. What is the best response?
optionC: Tear up the ticket and leave
optionD: Stay calm and finish the job
explanation: Insults alone are not a crime, and reacting escalates the situation. Stay professional and finish the task.

question: Your sergeant gives an order you think is unwise but that is not illegal or unsafe. What should you do?
optionA: Follow it, then discuss it later
optionB: Refuse until it is fully explained
explanation: Lawful, safe orders are followed. Raise your concerns afterward through the chain of command.

question: A supervisor orders you to do something clearly illegal. What should you do?
optionB: Decline and report it up the chain
optionC: Obey it and complain afterward in writing
optionD: Ask your partner to do it instead
explanation: No order makes an illegal act lawful. Decline and report it to a higher supervisor.

question: You stop a car for speeding and find the driver is your neighbor. What should you do?
optionA: Let him go since you know him
optionB: Give a ticket to avoid favoritism
optionC: Handle it as for any driver
optionD: Ask him for a favor in return
explanation: Treat him exactly as you would a stranger. Letting him go or being harsher because you know him are both unfair.

question: You find a mistake in a report you already turned in. What should you do?
optionC: Wait to fix it until it goes to court
optionD: Tell a supervisor and correct it
explanation: Errors are corrected openly, usually with a supplemental report. Swapping the report quietly looks like falsifying it.

question: A lost child walks up to you at a busy festival. What should you do first?
optionA: Stay with the child and call it in
optionB: Send the child to the info booth
optionC: Tell the child to look for parents
optionD: Leave the child to search the crowd
explanation: Keep the child with you so the child is safe, and radio a description so the parents can be found. Never send a lost child off alone.

question: A friend asks you to run a license plate on the police computer for a personal reason. What should you do?
optionA: Run it if it is just this once
optionB: Refuse; it is for official use only
optionC: Run it but do not share the address
optionD: Ask a coworker to run it for you
explanation: Police databases are for official business only. Running a plate for a friend is misuse even if you keep the result to yourself.

question: You see another officer use clearly excessive force on a handcuffed suspect. What should you do?
explanation: Officers are expected to intervene to stop clearly excessive force and to report it. Staying silent is a failure of duty.

question: Two calls come in at once: a burglary in progress and a report of a bike stolen yesterday. Which do you handle first?
optionA: The stolen bike, since it is quicker
explanation: A crime in progress puts people at risk and offers a chance to catch the suspect. The old theft report can wait.

question: An elderly man keeps calling about noise that you cannot hear when you arrive. What is the best approach?
optionA: Check it and talk to him kindly
optionC: Warn him about making false reports
explanation: Check the complaint and treat him with respect. Repeated calls can point to a real problem or a need for other services.

question: Off duty in a store, you see a shoplifter. Your agency tells off-duty officers to act as good witnesses unless a life is in danger. What should you do?
optionB: Watch closely and call it in
optionC: Confront him and show your badge
optionD: Do nothing since you are off duty
explanation: Follow the policy: observe, get a good description and call on-duty officers. Acting alone off duty is risky for everyone.

question: A man you arrested spits at you, then stops resisting while handcuffed. What should you do?
optionA: Strike him once to stop it
optionB: Tighten the cuffs as a lesson
optionC: Use no more force; document it
optionD: Release him to cool things down
explanation: Once a person is controlled, more force is punishment, not control. Document the spitting, which can be charged.

question: A reporter at a scene asks you for the victim's name. What should you do?
optionA: Give the name if it's been confirmed
optionB: Give the name off the record
optionC: Tell him to search social media
optionD: Refer him to the information officer
explanation: Most agencies release information through a designated public information officer, after families are told.

question: Your partner is often late, and you have been covering for him. What is the best step?
optionA: Talk to him, then a supervisor
optionB: Keep covering for him to protect him
optionD: Ask for a new partner quietly
explanation: Raise it with him directly first, and go to a supervisor if it continues. Covering for him is dishonest.

question: A driver you stopped offers you money to forget the ticket. What should you do?
optionA: Laugh it off and write the ticket
optionB: Refuse and treat it as a bribe
optionC: Accept it and turn it in later
explanation: Offering money to an officer is bribery. Refuse it and document and report the offer.

question: A resident asks you for directions while you are on your way to a non-emergency call. What should you do?
optionA: Ignore the resident and drive on
optionD: Tell them to look it up online
explanation: A quick answer serves the public without delaying the call much. A long escort leaves the call waiting.

question: At a crash scene, a bystander is filming you but is not interfering. What should you do?
optionC: Make them delete the video at once
optionD: Let them film and keep working
explanation: In the United States people may generally record police in public places. Act only if the person interferes with the work.

question: At a domestic call, the caller now says through the closed door that everything is fine. What should you do?
optionB: Leave, because the caller canceled it
optionD: Ask dispatch to close the call
explanation: Victims are sometimes pressured to cancel. Make contact and confirm everyone is safe before you leave.

question: A new policy changes how evidence must be logged, and you prefer the old way. What should you do?
explanation: Policies apply once they take effect. You can suggest changes, but you follow the current rule.

question: While serving a search warrant at a house, you find a large amount of cash. What should you do?
optionA: Count it later back at the station
optionB: Leave it where it was found
optionC: Count and log it with a witness
optionD: Log an estimate of the total
explanation: Count and record cash right away, ideally with a witness or supervisor, so no one can question what was found.

question: A distraught mother is shouting and demanding that you find her missing son right now. What is the best response?
optionA: Tell her to calm down or leave
optionB: Promise her he will be found today
optionD: Stay calm and gather the details
explanation: Her fear is understandable. Calmly get a description and where he was last seen, and do not make promises you cannot keep.

question: You learn that a close friend on the force has been falsifying overtime records. What should you do?
optionB: Warn him privately and give him time
optionD: Wait to see if it happens again
explanation: Falsifying records is dishonesty that must be reported, whoever does it. Friendship does not change the duty.

question: You are guarding a crime scene, and a city council member asks to come in and look around. What should you do?
optionC: Let them in with an escort
optionD: Ask them to sign in first
explanation: Only people with a job to do at the scene may enter. Rank or office outside the investigation does not give access.

question: While writing your report, you cannot remember whether you asked a certain question during an interview. What should you write?
optionC: Only what you are sure of
explanation: A report must be truthful. Write what you know, and never fill a gap with something you are not sure happened.

question: A driver you stopped is upset and accuses you of stopping him because of his race. What should you do?
optionA: End the stop and drive away at once
optionB: Argue that you are not racist
optionD: Stay calm and explain the stop
explanation: Stay professional and explain the reason for the stop. Arguing or punishing the comment escalates things and is improper.

question: A crowd gathers and yells while you make an arrest. What is your priority?
optionA: Secure the suspect and get backup
optionC: Release the suspect to calm the crowd
explanation: Control the suspect and call for help so the scene stays safe. Explaining to the crowd can come later.

question: You are first at a scene where a man is bleeding heavily from a leg wound. What do you do first?
optionA: Look for the person who did it
explanation: Saving life comes first. Heavy bleeding can kill in minutes, so control it and get medics coming.

question: In front of the public, another officer tells a joke that mocks an ethnic group. What should you do?
optionA: Laugh along to keep the peace
optionB: Ignore it since it was a joke
optionC: Tell him it is not acceptable
explanation: Demeaning remarks damage public trust. Address it, and report it if it continues or the policy requires.

question: You realize you gave a crash victim the wrong case number. What should you do?
optionA: Wait for them to call about it
optionC: Note it in your file only
explanation: Fix your own mistake quickly so the person is not harmed by it.

question: A policy says officers may not tow a car from a private lot unless the lot's owner signs a request. A car has been parked overnight in a grocery store lot, and the manager calls but will not sign. What can the officer do under this policy?
optionA: Not tow it under this policy
optionB: Tow it, since the store called
optionD: Tow it if it blocks parking
explanation: The rule requires a signed request, and there is none. A phone call, time or blocked spaces do not replace the signature.

question: Car break-ins this month happened on Monday at 9 p.m., Wednesday at 9 p.m., Friday at 9 p.m., Monday at 9 p.m. and Wednesday at 9 p.m. If the pattern continues, when is the next one most likely?
explanation: The break-ins repeat Monday, Wednesday, Friday at 9 p.m. After Wednesday comes Friday.

question: You drive north on Oak Street, turn right onto 5th Avenue, then turn left onto Pine Street. Which way are you facing?
explanation: A right turn from north faces east, and a left turn from east faces north again.

question: You drive east, turn right, then turn right again. Which way are you heading?
explanation: Right from east is south, and right from south is west.

question: An evidence procedure says: photograph the item, measure its location, collect it, then package and label it. Which step comes right after measuring?
explanation: The order is photograph, measure, collect, package and label. Collecting follows measuring.

question: Two witnesses say the getaway car was a red sedan, the plate is registered to a red sedan, and a store camera shows a red SUV. Which piece of information does not fit the others?
explanation: Three sources agree on a red sedan. The camera's SUV is the one that conflicts and needs follow-up.

question: All officers on the night watch have finished crisis training. Officer Park has not finished crisis training. Which must be true?
optionA: Park is on the day watch
optionC: Park is not on the night watch
optionD: No one on days has the training
explanation: If Park were on nights, he would have the training. He could be on days or swing, so day watch is not certain.

question: House numbers on one side of a block run 102, 106, 110, 114. What is the next number?
explanation: Each number is 4 more than the one before, so 114 plus 4 is 118.

question: A rule says a supervisor must respond to any call where force is used or a person is injured. Which call needs a supervisor?
optionA: A suspect scrapes a knee fleeing
optionB: A loud party is broken up
optionC: A driver gets a speeding ticket
explanation: A scraped knee is an injury, so the rule applies. The others involve no force and no injury.

question: Headquarters is two blocks east of the courthouse. The jail is one block north of headquarters. The hospital is three blocks west of the jail. Where is the hospital from the courthouse?
explanation: Two east, then three west, leaves one block west. The one block north stays. So the hospital is one west and one north.

question: Two suspects have the same build and wear the same clothes. Which detail would best tell them apart?
optionA: The color of the jeans they wore
optionC: A tattoo on one man's neck
explanation: A tattoo belongs to one person and stays with him. Clothes, build and direction are shared or change.

question: If an alarm sounds and the keyholder does not answer, the officer checks the outside of the building. If the outside is secure, the alarm is logged as false. The keyholder did not answer, and the officer found a broken rear window. What follows?
optionA: The alarm is logged as false
optionC: The officer must leave the scene
optionD: The alarm is not logged as false
explanation: A false log needs a secure building, and a broken window means it is not secure.

question: Case numbers follow a pattern: 26-0101, 26-0103, 26-0105. What is the next case number?
explanation: The number goes up by 2 each time and the year part stays 26.

question: Of 40 complaints about a noisy bar, 30 came on Fridays and Saturdays. When should extra patrols be scheduled?
explanation: Three quarters of the complaints come on those two days, so that is where patrols do the most good.

question: A victim says she was robbed at 9:30 p.m. The suspect's bus pass was scanned at 9:28 p.m. across town, a 40-minute trip from the scene. What does this suggest?
optionA: The suspect used a car to get there
optionC: It casts doubt on the suspect
explanation: If he had the pass, he could not reach the scene in 2 minutes. It weakens the case but does not prove someone else used the pass.

question: To join the bike unit, an officer needs two years of service and a passed fitness test. Officer Cruz has three years of service but failed the fitness test. Is Cruz eligible?
optionA: Yes, the service requirement is met
optionC: No, three years is too many
explanation: The rule uses and, so both conditions must be met. Cruz fails the fitness condition.

question: You face west, turn around 180 degrees, then turn 90 degrees to your left. Which way do you face?
explanation: Turning around from west faces east. A left turn from east faces north.

question: Records are filed alphabetically by last name. Which name is filed first?
explanation: Compare letter by letter: Mab comes before Mac, and Mac comes before Mc.

question: Three robberies were at gas stations between 1 and 3 a.m., each by one man in a blue mask. A fourth robbery is at a pharmacy at noon by two women. What is the best conclusion?
optionA: It is the same robber as before
optionB: The man has new partners now
optionC: It is probably a separate case
explanation: Place, time and suspects all differ from the pattern, so the fourth robbery is most likely unrelated.

question: A policy lets emergency vehicles exceed the speed limit only with lights and siren on. Officer Hall drove 15 mph over the limit with lights on but no siren. Did she follow the policy?
optionD: No, the siren was also needed
explanation: The policy requires both lights and siren. Lights alone do not meet it.

question: A witness says: "The man had a beard, wore a red cap and was very tall, and I think he got into a car, but I was looking at my phone." Which part is least reliable?
optionA: That he got into a car
optionC: That he wore a red cap
explanation: The witness hedges only about the car and admits looking at a phone at that moment.

question: Unit 1 is 4 miles from a call and Unit 2 is 6 miles away, both able to drive 40 mph. Unit 3 is 3 miles away but stuck in traffic at 15 mph. Which unit arrives first?
explanation: Unit 1 takes 6 minutes, Unit 2 takes 9 and Unit 3 takes 12. Closest is not always fastest.

question: Over six months, thefts from cars rose on blocks with broken streetlights and fell on blocks where the lights were repaired. What is the most reasonable conclusion?
